glosses: To cause to become.

examples.text: The shot rendered her immobile.

[…] St. Bede's at this period of its history was perhaps the poorest and most miserable parish in the East End of London. Close-packed, crushed by the buttressed height of the railway viaduct, rendered airless by huge walls of factories, it at once banished lively interest from a stranger's mind and left only a dull oppression of the spirit.

This service has suffered badly from Department for Transport-inspired cuts which reduced it from hourly to two-hourly. This, coupled with regular cancellations, has rendered the train service between the area's two biggest towns almost unusable.

examples.text: For catching the thief, you'll get a nice reward.

glosses: A prize promised for a certain deed or catch

examples.text: The rewards for bringing in badly wanted criminals are printed on 'dead or alive' posters.

glosses: The result of an action, whether good or bad.

examples.text: Is this the reward I get for telling the truth: to be put in jail?

glosses: To give a reward to or for.

examples.text: Why are you rewarding the child for misbehaving?

glosses: To be a recompense for.

examples.text: Decorations are meant to reward the most meritous acts and services.

Bulgaria gave a hint of defensive frailties to come when they failed to clear Young's corner, and when Gareth Barry found Cahill in the box he applied the finish past Nikolay Mihaylov.

glosses: To give (something) as a reward.

examples.text:
Thenne syr Marhaus departed and within two dayes his damoysel brought hym where as was a grete tornement that the lady de Vawse has cryed
[…]

 & had somtyme doune fourty knyghtes
 and soo the serklet of gold was rewarded hym

glosses: An equivalent returned for anything given, done, or suffered; compensation; reward; amends; requital.
That which compensates for an injury, or other type of harm or damage.

examples.text: He offered money as recompense for the damage, but what the injured party wanted was an apology.

O let my books be then the eloquence
And dumb presagers of my speaking breast,
Who plead for love and look for recompense
More than that tongue that more hath more express'd.

glosses: To reward or repay (someone) for something done, given etc.

examples.text: She in regard thereof him recompenst / With golden words, and goodly countenance, / And such fond fauours sparingly dispenst […]

glosses: To give compensation for an injury, or other type of harm or damage.

examples.text: The judge ordered the defendant to recompense the plaintiff by paying $100.

glosses: To give (something) in return; to pay back; to pay, as something earned or deserved.

examples.text: Recompense to no man evil for evil.

glosses: To do something harmful or negative to get revenge for some harm; to fight back or respond in kind to an injury or affront.

examples.text: John insulted Peter to retaliate for Peter's acid remark earlier.
Many companies have policies in place to prevent bosses from retaliating against allegations of harassment.

glosses: To repay or requite by an act of the same kind.

examples.text: One ambassador sent word to the duke's son that his visit should be retaliated.

glosses: Causar derechos los géneros que se introducen.
